lines.text: Bear's Notes The Ultraviolet Catastrophe
Heat any object and it glows, and physics in
1900 could predict that glow.
The prediction was not "very bright" — it was
infinitely bright.
Taken literally, the warm walls of your room should
blast you with ultraviolet light.
They don't, so something inside perfectly good physics is
broken — let's find where.
Picture light trapped in a box, rattling back and
forth as standing waves.
At low frequency, only a few wave patterns fit
inside the box.
Raise the frequency and far more patterns fit —
the count climbs like frequency squared.
Classical physics then hands every pattern the exact same
share of energy.
A few cheap patterns, then a rising flood of
them, each one fully funded.
Multiply the exploding count by that fixed share, and
the predicted glow races upward.
Plot it, and the curve climbs without limit straight
into the ultraviolet.
But measure a real hot object, and its glow
rises, peaks, then gently falls.
Two curves for one object:
one screams to infinity, the other comes home to
zero.
So which honest-looking step in that argument was actually
the lie?
Not the counting — the geometry of standing waves
in a box is rock solid.
The culprit is the quiet assumption that a pattern
can hold any energy, down to slivers.
Planck's desperate remedy:
a pattern's energy comes only in whole chunks.
Each chunk is worth a tiny new constant, h,
times how fast the wave wiggles.
Low-frequency chunks are cheap, so nothing changes where classical
physics already worked.
But high-frequency chunks are expensive — ultraviolet light is
billed in costly lumps.
A warm object simply cannot afford those costly ultraviolet
chunks.
So the expensive patterns stay empty, and the runaway
curve bends back down to zero.
The catastrophe was never real — it was the
price of pretending energy is smooth.
One ratio decides everything:
the chunk's cost against the warmth available.
When warmth dwarfs the chunk it looks classical;
when the chunk wins, it looks quantum.
That single rule — energy in whole chunks —
is the seed of all quantum physics.
We didn't derive Planck's exact curve, and we left
light's own graininess for next time.
Try this yourself:
estimate a chunk's cost for green light, and weigh
it against room-temperature warmth.
Thanks for watching The Ultraviolet Catastrophe — more at
youtube dot com, slash, at Nik Bear Brown.
